title: Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh
hook: a father and son executed in Lahore in 1745 for refusing to give up their faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh, two horses tied outside the gate at Amritsar. Your line was they rode in. Today, a quieter kind of courage, in Lahore. Go gently with this one.

Some people live between two worlds. They work inside a system and belong to a community that system is hunting. They translate, they carry messages, they try to keep both sides talking. Subeg Singh was one of those people. Tradition says he was a Sikh who held a post with the government in Lahore, trusted enough to be sent with messages to the Khalsa. He had a son, Shahbaz Singh, a young man with his life ahead of him.
screen: `BETWEEN TWO WORLDS.` → `A SIKH WITH A POST IN LAHORE.` → `A SON WITH HIS LIFE AHEAD.`

segments.voice: For a while, Subeg Singh's position kept his family safe. He was useful. He was a bridge. But the hunted years turned harder, and a bridge takes the strain from both sides. Tradition says the trouble began with the son. Shahbaz Singh was pressed to give up his faith, and he refused. Then the father was arrested too. Both were brought before the authorities in Lahore, and both, tradition says, were offered the same thing: their lives, if they would leave the Sikh path. What makes this story so hard to hear comes next. Tradition says the authorities did not only threaten them; they tried to use them against each other. A father can be broken through his son, a son through his father. Surely one of them would give way to save the other. Neither did. Tradition says they were put on the wheel, the charkhri, a torture that Sikhs name in the Ardas, the standing prayer, when they remember those who were broken on wheels and did not give up their faith. Tradition counts Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh among them, together. What the tradition dwells on is not only the pain. It's the strange kind of love in it. Either might have given his life for the other. What neither would do was ask the other to give up his faith. They held each other up by holding on: father and son, side by side, each making the same refusal, and each, in a way, making it easier for the other.
screen: `A BRIDGE BETWEEN TWO WORLDS.` · `THE SON REFUSES. THE FATHER IS TAKEN.` · `USED AGAINST EACH OTHER.` · `NEITHER GIVES WAY.` · then, large: `FATHER AND SON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a father and a son you know, maybe your own father, maybe your son, maybe a pair you've watched from a distance, close or estranged, and see them side by side. Notice what they carry for each other, and what lies between them. If you pray, hold them before Waheguru, saying the Name on each breath out; if you don't, just wish them well, breath by breath.
Subeg Singh. A father in Lahore, offered his life to give up his faith alongside his son Shahbaz Singh; neither would, and tradition counts them among the martyrs the Ardas recalls.
Your line: father and son. Neither one asked the other to let go of his faith. Rest gently tonight.

notes: Subeg Singh's government post (often described as a contractor or official in Lahore, and as the go-between for the nawabship offer of day 852) is kept general. Confirm.

The tradition that the trouble began at Shahbaz Singh's school, with his teacher pressing him to convert, is deliberately kept general ('pressed to give up his faith') to avoid making another tradition the foil. A Keeper may want the fuller version told carefully.
Tellings differ on whether the son or the father was arrested first and on the details of the wheel. Confirm.
'Tried to use them against each other' is an interpretation of the tradition that each was urged to save the other; confirm it is fair.
The Ardas line on those broken on wheels is paraphrased, not quoted.
The year (in the index hook) is left out of the voice under the claims rule.
